WalkthroughText: When you assign one reference variable to another (like b = a for Strings, or copy = nums for arrays), you are copying the arrow that points into the heap — not the object itself. Both variables become aliases pointing at the exact same heap object, so changes made through one alias are visible through the other, as long as that object is mutable, like an array. Strings, however, are immutable: methods like toLowerCase() or concat() never change the characters inside an existing String object. Instead they build a brand-new String object somewhere else in the heap and hand back a reference to it, so reassigning a variable to that result breaks the alias rather than mutating shared data. Keeping the refArrow + heapObject + indexedStrip picture in mind — arrows from variables into boxes in the heap, with indexed array boxes able to change their contents in place — is the key to correctly reasoning about aliasing versus immutability on the exam.

Choices: HELLO hello, because b.toLowerCase() creates a brand-new String object that b now refers to, leaving a's object unchanged
hello hello, because a and b are aliases for the same object, so changing b also changes a
HELLO HELLO, because String methods never actually change the value stored in memory
hello hello, because toLowerCase() modifies the object in place at the address both a and b point to
PracticeItems.Explanation: Strings are immutable in Java. b = b.toLowerCase() does not alter the original "HELLO" object; it creates a new String object "hello" and reassigns the reference variable b to point at it. The variable a still points to the original "HELLO" object, so a and b now point to two different heap objects. The correct output is 'HELLO hello'. The distractors incorrectly assume aliasing persists after reassignment or that Strings can be mutated in place.

Arrays are objects, so copy = nums makes copy an alias for the SAME array object as nums (both refArrows point to the same indexedStrip in the heap). Math.abs(-3) evaluates to 3, so copy[1] becomes 45 + 3 = 48. Since nums and copy reference the identical array, nums[1] is also 48. The distractor '45' would only be correct if copy were an independent deep copy, which it is not.

concat appends "nap" to produce a brand new String object "catnap" and reassigns s1's reference to it, so s1 no longer equals "cat". s2 still refers to a separate heap object holding "cat". Since s1 now holds "catnap" and s2 holds "cat", s1.equals(s2) is false (different contents) and s1 == s2 is false (different objects entirely, and even different content). The distractor 'true false' wrongly assumes s1 still equals "cat".

WalkthroughSteps.Caption: Let's start by declaring a String variable a set to "HELLO". This creates a heap object holding the characters H-E-L-L-O, and a reference arrow from variable a points to it.
Now we declare b and assign it a. This does NOT create a new object — it just copies the arrow, so b becomes an alias pointing at the very same heap object as a.
Next we call b.toLowerCase(). Since Strings are immutable, this method cannot change the letters inside the existing HELLO object — it must build a brand new object.
The result of toLowerCase() is assigned back to b, so b's arrow is redirected to point at the new lowercase object, while a's arrow still points at the original HELLO object.

Notice the two arrows now point to two separate heap objects: a still points to HELLO, and b points to hello. This is why printing a and b gives different results, even though they started out aliased.
Now compare that to an array scenario. We create an int array nums holding 12, 45, 7, 9 — this is our indexedStrip in the heap.
We declare copy and assign it nums. Just like before, this only copies the arrow — copy becomes a true alias for the same array object, not a separate copy of the data.
Now we compute copy[1] = copy[1] + Math.abs(-3). Math.abs(-3) resolves to 3, and copy[1] was 45, so the new value is 48.
Because copy and nums are aliases pointing at the SAME indexedStrip, writing 48 into index 1 through copy changes the shared array — nums[1] becomes 48 too, unlike the String example.
